title: Milton Keynes City Council pilots the Valon AI planning platform from October to December 2025, reports receipt-to-validation time falling from 15.8 to 7.6 days and buys a one-year license
summary: Milton Keynes City Council reports that receipt-to-validation time for planning applications fell from 15.8 to 7.6 days while its officers piloted the Valon AI planning platform.
account: Milton Keynes piloted Valon for planning work from October to December 2025. The council reports that officers validated applications 60–80% faster. Its analysis of the planning register put average receipt-to-validation time at 15.8 days before and 7.6 days during the pilot, and validation-to-decision time at 53.1 and 43.2 days. The council writes that it built its evidence base from officer timesheets and data from the public planning register. The estimated 1,360 officer hours per year is an extrapolation from an assumed 80% saving. Valon’s own account describes major-application checks falling from about 65 to 10 minutes and non-major checks from 15 to 5 minutes. It reports 7.7 days for early-November validation turnaround and a separate 18% decision-time difference against a non-pilot group. Neither account publishes the underlying timesheets, selected application records, sample sizes, or rules for constructing the comparisons. The gains are reported, and how much of them the AI caused is uncertain. The council purchased a one-year license after the pilot and reports continued use (Local Government Association case study, 8 May 2026). Integration with Arcus is being scoped, and rollout to all planning officers remains an ambition.
purpose: Support planning officers from application validation through decision-making.

fields.summary: Milton Keynes City Council reports that receipt-to-validation time for planning applications fell from 15.8 to 7.6 days while its officers piloted the Valon AI planning platform.
fields.account: Milton Keynes piloted Valon for planning work from October to December 2025. The council reports that officers validated applications 60–80% faster. Its analysis of the planning register put average receipt-to-validation time at 15.8 days before and 7.6 days during the pilot, and validation-to-decision time at 53.1 and 43.2 days. The council writes that it built its evidence base from officer timesheets and data from the public planning register. The estimated 1,360 officer hours per year is an extrapolation from an assumed 80% saving. Valon’s own account describes major-application checks falling from about 65 to 10 minutes and non-major checks from 15 to 5 minutes. It reports 7.7 days for early-November validation turnaround and a separate 18% decision-time difference against a non-pilot group. Neither account publishes the underlying timesheets, selected application records, sample sizes, or rules for constructing the comparisons. The gains are reported, and how much of them the AI caused is uncertain. The council purchased a one-year license after the pilot and reports continued use (Local Government Association case study, 8 May 2026). Integration with Arcus is being scoped, and rollout to all planning officers remains an ambition.
